Made me laugh:

A Frenchman, an Englishman, and a German were each commissioned to conduct a study of the camel.

The Frenchman went to the Jardin des Plantes, spent half an hour there, questioned the keeper, threw some bread to the camel, teased it with the tip of his umbrella, and then went home and wrote, for his newspaper, a lively column full of witty and incisive observations.

The Englishman, taking along his tea basket and a comfortable set of camping equipment, went off to pitch his tent in the lands of the East. After spending two or three years there, he returned with a hefty volume crammed with facts, without much order or any conclusion, but of genuine documentary value.

As for the German, full of contempt for the Frenchman’s frivolity and the Englishman’s lack of general ideas, he shut himself up in his room to write a work in several volumes entitled: The Idea of the Camel Derived from the Conception of the Self.

This is interesting work to think about the long-run case. I am trying to wrap my head around how possible this is in practice outside of just a steady-state environment.

The ~5x wage increase comes with an ~8x rise in output per worker and a gross savings rate going from ~20% to ~40% (?) of output if I have that right? The wage gain therefore then seems to be mostly produced by the productivity event.

Over the last two decades while capital share has risen materially, labor productivity growth has sat constant at 1.5–2%. Does that discredit this analysis by implying a loss in bargaining power for labor or some other driving force rather than a technological revolution?

Another question I'd be curious your views on is that I believe this assumes capital and labor remain complements? If AI actually starts to replace workers and increases the elasticity of substitution, would it then threaten the rise in labor's productivity/compensation?

In politics I guess the transitional dynamics you mention are sometimes the most important part as that starts to bring a multitude of other factors into the environment (eg immigration and work force demographics).

$HGRAF
September 30, 2026

I bought heavily into HydroGraph before today’s close. The selling looked to me like short pressure triggering stop losses—and I used the weakness to increase my position.

Why such strong conviction? Look at the commercial setup entering Q4.

🔹 Larger orders on the horizon. HydroGraph’s latest MD&A says customer discussions are expected to generate larger purchase orders AND a long-term supply agreement within calendar 2026. Management still has to deliver, but that makes the coming quarter particularly interesting.

🔹 Plastics alone offer enormous potential. Automotive components, packaging, electronics and consumer goods all need lighter, stronger, more durable materials. HydroGraph reports thermoplastic test examples showing 30% higher strength at break and 60% greater toughness. These are benefits manufacturers have a reason to evaluate.

🔹 The commercial infrastructure is taking shape. Hubron, Broadway, Modern Dispersions and Midland are qualified compounding partners—helping integrate graphene into usable polymer formulations and providing routes into established industrial supply chains.

🔹 Fresh evidence from coatings. Sparc’s September 15 announcement reported a 25% improvement in corrosion resistance in 16-week solvent-based coating tests using HydroGraph graphene. Longer testing is due in November; positive results would lead to commercial supply negotiations.

🔹 Defense adds another major opportunity. HydroGraph is pursuing applications across government, aerospace and defense, with former Hexcel executive Dr. Robert Yancey developing those relationships. Qualification takes time, but the potential extends across advanced composites, coatings and other demanding applications.

What excites me is the breadth: automotive, plastics, coatings, concrete, thermal management, etc. There is so much, just take a look at the graphics below to get an idea. The paste and compounding strategy help customers overcome the practical barriers to adoption.

My conviction is that successful adoption in even a few of these markets could create a substantial recurring business. Meaningful orders still need to land, but the groundwork is increasingly tangible.

What happens when one major manufacturer qualifies an additive that improves its products—and competitors need to catch up?

That’s the possibility I’m buying into.

While it isn't all about the quid pro quo between the company and the employee, this balance must be economically viable for the relationships to be sustainable. 

Set policies that clearly define this quid pro quo, and be measured, but not excessively precise, when shifting it around. While you should by and large stick to the arrangement, you should also recognize that there are rare, special times when employees will need a bit of extra time off and there are times that the company will require employees to give it extra hours. The company should pay for above-normal work one way or another, and employees should be docked for below-normal work. 

The give-and-take should roughly equal out over time. #principleoftheday

After 3 years building LLM agents, I think the model people actually choose to run says a lot, it’s a bit like voting with your credit card. That’s why the benchmark I pay the most attention to is usage on OpenRouter.

For smaller/cheaper models, DeepSeek Flash is doing ~22.7T tokens a week, GLM Flash ~10.6T and GPT-6 Luna ~5.1T, which gives you a pretty good idea of where people are finding value for money.

For larger, frontier models, Opus 5.5 is at ~1.9T and GPT-6 Sol ~1.2T, while Gemini Pro is at ~0.2T, roughly 10x less volume than Opus.

Obviously cheaper models will consume more tokens, so you have to compare within each category, but I find this much more useful than another benchmark showing a model winning by 2 points. You can game a benchmark but not where companies are spending their $$$.

And that still only gives you the global trend. For your product, the eval that matters is your own, on actual customer tasks, because a model can be amazing overall and still suck at the specific thing you need it to do.

That’s why I think you want a multi-model platform, with customer evals driving which model handles which task, so you can improve quality and optimize your token stack as the models change. You shouldn’t be married to one model.

When software becomes a commodity, the moat is how much value you deliver per unit of compute.

Anyone can build the same features. Few can serve as many users, across as many use cases, without restrictive limits.

Model quality compounds that advantage: better results with less compute mean higher gross margins and more compute to train the next, more efficient model.

That’s the winning flywheel for the next 24 months.
